extracted.intended_audience: general educated readers of literary/philosophical essays; writers of personal/self-examining essays
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and principles for composing frank, self-reflective personal essays and for judging character, learning, and public conduct as exemplified in a Montaigne-style essay of self-examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Candour: speak what you think
rubrics_metrics.description: “A man must not always tell all, for that were folly: but what a man says should be what he thinks, otherwise ‘tis knavery.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer honesty over dissembling; examples and admonitions against pretending to conceal one's thoughts or habitually counterfeiting. The essayist states a preference to be 'troublesome and indiscreet' rather than a flatterer and dissembler, arguing that persistent dissembling destroys credibility and usefulness in conversation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrity of promise: avoid breaking faith for short gain
rubrics_metrics.description: Breaking one's word for present advantage brings long-term disrepute and distrust: “Gain tempts to the first breach of faith... throwing this prince out of all correspondence and negotiation, by this example of infidelity.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anecdote of Soliman ordering the release of prisoners despite a capitulation breach illustrates that even seemingly useful breaches harm future negotiations; consequence-based argument against sacrificing faith/conscience for momentary benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer truthfulness over political expediency
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who value affairs over faith and conscience may defend momentary breaches, but repeated infidelity produces infinite prejudice and loss of correspondence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied especially to rulers/princes: short-term success from lying undermines future governance and relations; the moral point doubles as practical counsel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge and accommodate limited memory
rubrics_metrics.description: “Memory is a faculty of wonderful use... for my part I have none at all.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical adaptations: use notes for commissions, learn long speeches word-for-word if necessary, keep discourse close and avoid digressions that one cannot hold in memory. Examples: forgetting watchwords, needing others to remember/library reminders; the writer recommends relying on writing/notes when memory fails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept and own your defects in public writing/speech
rubrics_metrics.description: “I am not obliged not to utter absurdities, provided I am not deceived in them and know them to be such.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is acceptable to publish or speak apparent absurdities so long as one is honest about them; the author embraces his own follies and deficiencies rather than feigning perfection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Candour beats affectation in social conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: The author prefers candour and openness, even at risk of incivility, because he lacks the art to dissemble convincingly: he 'abandon[s] himself to candour, always to speak as I think.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you cannot maintain an acted truth (no memory, no assurance, no art of evasion), be candid rather than perform a falsehood that you cannot sustain; anecdotal examples show forced conviviality backfiring (e.g., inability to drink on command).

rubrics_metrics.name: When indecisive, defer to chance or stronger conviction
rubrics_metrics.description: “I can maintain an opinion, but I cannot choose one... I could willingly refer it to be decided by the chance of a die.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If human reasons for two options are evenly balanced, it is reasonable to let fortune decide or to follow those more confident in their opinions; the author frames indecision as tolerable and sometimes prudent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education should form virtue/prudence, not merely erudition
rubrics_metrics.description: “The end of which is not to render us good and wise, but learned... She has not taught us to follow and embrace virtue and prudence, but she has imprinted in us their derivation and etymology.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique of schooling that trains to define and name virtues without producing the habits or love of them; implication for writers/teachers: favor works and instruction that cultivate character and practical wisdom over mere display of learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical, local knowledge is often superior to abstract learning
rubrics_metrics.description: “Plus sapit vulgus, quia tantum, quantum opus est, sapit.” — 'The vulgar are so much the wiser, because they only know what is needful for them to know.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Country manners and plain knowledge are better adapted to the use of life than empty erudition; value simplicity and usefulness in judgment and conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be wary of scholars' vanity and overreach
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who profess the greatest abilities often expose disproportion and defects when they advance things without discretion; scholars may disgrace their work by ill handling and treating all authorities alike.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't overapply learned authorities or display erudition at the expense of judgment; measure claims to the worth of the subject and avoid honoring all authorities equally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give honest, proportionate praise
rubrics_metrics.description: “What I see that is fine in others I very readily commend... but to attribute to them qualities that they have not, I cannot do it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author will praise more than he privately thinks when deserved, but refuses to invent virtues; advice: praise candidly but avoid false encomium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value steadiness and established practice over restless change
rubrics_metrics.description: “...in public affairs, there is no government so ill, provided it be ancient and has been constant, that is not better than change and alteration.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Skeptical counsel about reforms: destabilizing established customs and laws risks worse outcomes; preservation and caution are virtues in political prudence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for universality and readiness of soul
rubrics_metrics.description: “The beautiful souls are they that are universal, open, and ready for all things; if not instructed, at least capable of being so.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ideal character and, by extension, ideal writers, cultivate breadth, openness, and capacity to learn; being universally receptive is preferable to narrow specialization.

rubrics_metrics.name: A writer's recognition depends partly on learned authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: The learned judge books primarily by learning and erudition; ignorance of classical authorities (e.g., Aristotle) is held against an author by some readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that one audience values classical learning and precise scholarship; if addressing that audience, attend to technical correctness and citation; but also recognize other audiences value different qualities (practical wisdom, plain speech).
